t: Implementation: changeover, data conversion and training
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson AP08: Implementation: changeover, data conversion and training.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Describe what implementation involves and why it must be planned. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Implementation is the stage at which a newly developed system is put into operation and replaces whatever was used before, whether an older computer system or a paper-based one. It has to be planned while the system is still being developed, because a lot has to be ready before the new system can take over completely: hardware and networks must be installed, software set up, staff trained and documentation provided. Existing data usually has to be converted into a form the new system can use. The organisation must then choose how to move from the old system to the new one.
Makes sense. Keep going.

There are four changeover methods: parallel, where old and new run side by side; direct, where the old system stops and the new one starts on a set date; pilot, where the whole system is tried in one section first; and phased, where parts of the system are introduced one at a time. Each balances risk against cost and time differently, so the right choice depends on the organisation. After implementation, the system will need ongoing maintenance throughout its life.
Right. What else do we need to know?

In parallel changeover the old and new systems operate together for a period. Every transaction is processed by both, and the two sets of results are checked against each other to confirm the new system gives correct output. When the new system has proved reliable, the old one is stopped. This is the safest method, because if the new system turns out to have flaws the old system is still there as a backup, and staff can become familiar with the new system gradually.
Got it. Keep going.

However, it is expensive and time-consuming to keep two systems running, checking one against the other takes extra effort, and two separate copies of the data have to be kept, which may fall out of step. Direct changeover, sometimes called the big bang approach, switches off the old system on a particular date and introduces the new one immediately. There is no duplication of resources and everyone starts using the new system together. It is very risky, though: should the new system break down, going back to the old one may be difficult or impossible, and there may be a period when no system is available.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Pilot changeover introduces the complete new system in one department, branch or section of the organisation first. The rest of the organisation keeps using the old system until the pilot has shown that the new one works, after which it is rolled out everywhere else. It suits organisations with several similar sections, such as a building society with many branches or a retailer with many shops. Only one section is affected if problems arise, and the staff in the pilot section gain experience that lets them help train others.
Okay. Keep going.

Its drawbacks are that two systems run at the same time in different parts of the organisation, which needs extra resources, and it may be difficult to share data between sections using different systems. Phased changeover introduces the system one component at a time, for example payroll first, then invoicing, checking each part works before the next is switched on. Staff face change in stages, which can be less stressful, and a problem should affect only one part. However, the full changeover can take a long time, and requests to alter parts already introduced can delay the rest.
Go on.

Because failure during changeover can be costly, organisations look for the lowest-risk method they can afford that is actually feasible. Where an organisation has several similar sites, pilot changeover is often a good balance, since it limits risk to one site without the full cost of parallel running. Where the consequences of failure would be severe, such as possible injury or major financial loss, parallel running may be justified despite its higher cost, because the old system remains as a safety net. Phased changeover suits a system made of distinct parts that can be introduced independently.
Right. Keep going.

Direct changeover carries the most risk and is used only when there is no realistic alternative, for example when the old and new systems cannot run at the same time, or for a small and non-critical system. A famous example of an unavoidable direct change was Sweden switching from driving on the left to driving on the right on a single morning in 1967: running both at once was impossible, so the change was planned in great detail months in advance. Direct changeover should be timed for a quiet period, with staff fully trained beforehand.
Go on.

Data conversion is the task of transferring existing records into the structure and format the new system expects, so that it can be used fully from the start. When a computer system replaces a paper-based one, records such as forms, reports, orders and invoices must be turned into electronic data. This usually means creating the new database structure, employing staff to type in or scan the paper records, and then verifying and validating the data that has been entered. Verification might involve proof-reading entries against the original documents or keying data in twice, while validation rules reject impossible values.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The volume of work can be large, particularly if scanned images of documents are to be stored. Where the new system replaces an older computer system, transferring the data, sometimes called data migration, is normally quicker, but fields may need reformatting, for example changing date formats or splitting a full name into first name and surname, and specialised or bespoke conversion software may be required. Poorly converted data causes errors and undermines users’ confidence in the new system.
Go on.

Users need training so that they can use the new system confidently and are more likely to accept it rather than resist it. Instructor-led classroom training allows questions and hands-on practice and gives everyone the same message, but it is expensive and takes staff away from their work. One-to-one or on-the-job training can be tailored to each person and uses real tasks, but it is slow and costly for large numbers. E-learning, video tutorials and online help let staff learn at their own pace and revisit material, and are cheap per person once produced, but offer no immediate help with problems and rely on staff being motivated.
Got it. Keep going.

Printed manuals are cheap and useful for later reference but are often left unread. Cascade training, in which a few staff are trained and then train their colleagues, suits large organisations spread across many sites, although quality may fall at each level. Training must fit the changeover method: direct changeover needs everyone trained before the switch, whereas pilot staff can become the trainers for later sites.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Implementation?
The stage at which a new system is put into operation, including installation, data conversion, training, documentation and changeover from the old system.
Changeover?
The process of moving from an old system to a new system, using a planned method: parallel, direct, pilot or phased.
Parallel changeover?
A changeover method in which the old and new systems run at the same time on the same transactions so that outputs can be compared until the new system is proven.
Direct changeover?
A changeover method in which the old system stops and the new one takes over at a single moment, with no overlap.
Pilot changeover?
A changeover method in which the whole new system is introduced in one branch, department or site before being extended to every other part of the organisation.
Phased changeover?
A changeover method in which the new system is introduced one component or function at a time.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Describe questions on changeover methods usually give a mark for what the method is and further marks for a benefit and a drawback, so learn at least one of each for all four methods. Evaluate or justify questions need you to apply advantages and disadvantages to the scenario and reach a reasoned recommendation; a general list with no link to the business earns limited credit. Phrase your answer around the organisation, for example explaining that parallel running is justified for payroll because an error would mean staff are paid wrongly. Classification questions describe a situation, often outside computing, and ask which method it shows. Look for the key feature: one location first means pilot, one part at a time means phased, both running together means parallel, and an overnight switch with no overlap means direct. The most common mistake is to confuse pilot and phased, so remember that pilot is the whole system in one place while phased is part of the system everywhere. For data conversion, refer to the actual records in the scenario, such as a diary or receipt book, and explain how they become tables in the new system.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A council introduces its new planning system in its Omagh office before all its other offices. Which method is this? Is it A, Phased; B, Direct; C, Pilot; D, Parallel?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: Pilot. The whole system is used in one site first, then rolled out to the rest.
That's it for Implementation: changeover, data conversion and training. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
